book.Title: {{W|On the Founding of Places}}
book.page:
{{C|Of the Basin}}
You will want a founder's basin, which is a shallow tin thing of no particular worth, kept by the sort of trader who deals in rope and salt and other unglamorous necessities. Any vessel would serve. The basin is traditional because it is wide, and because everyone can see into it.
Fill it with fresh water — eight drams is the customary measure, being enough that the pouring is felt — and set it down on ground you mean to keep. Then pour, and name the place aloud, and drink with whoever is standing there.
The ground is claimed from that moment. Not by law; there is no law out here. By the fact that water was shared on it in front of witnesses.

{{C|What Follows, and in What Order}}
{{W|First, beds.}} Settlers walk a long way on rumor. If there is nowhere to sleep when they arrive, they will look at your ground, and think about their feet, and keep walking. No place ever grew past the number of beds in it.
{{W|Second, water held.}} Not water passing through — water {{C|kept}}. A settlement is measured by what it can store against a dry month. Casks, then a cistern. Dedicate them openly, so the water-keepers know which vessels are the settlement's and which are merely someone's.
{{W|Third, hands.}} A mill with nobody at it is a pile of good timber. Count your people before you commission the works, or watch them stand idle.

{{C|A Warning, Cheerfully Given}}
The world will notice. It always does.
Some who notice will want to trade with you, and some will want to be paid not to trouble you, and a few will simply come. This is not a failure of your rule. It is the price of existing somewhere that other people can find.
Pay the tribute if the tribute is cheaper than the raid. Write down what happens either way. Two hundred years from now the writing is the only part that will still be there.
